html:
User Acceptance Testing (UAT) is where the business proves the delivered solution with real data and real scenarios, on its own schedule and by its own rules. This phase covers writing the UAT plan, designing test cases that mirror actual BrightLogistics work, logging defects when expected results do not happen, and gating go-live behind a formal sign-off. Every test case traces back to a requirement, so "it works" becomes something the business can verify rather than something the project team claims.

By the end you will be able to take the design decisions from Phase 11, turn them into a runnable UAT cycle on the UAT_Test_Case__c object, and present a Go/No-Go recommendation that a business owner can sign with confidence.

Learning Objectives

  • Write a UAT plan from the approved acceptance criteria, ...
  • Design test cases that mirror real business flows, ...
  • Track defects with severity and priority, ...
  • Gate go-live on formal sign-off, ...
  • Trace every test case back to a requirement and a user story, ...
  • Run a UAT cycle with daily triage and clean retesting, ...
  • Use the defect logging flow without fixing in the middle of a cycle, ...
  • Hand a signed UAT result forward into change management, ...

1. What UAT Is and Is Not

UAT is the phase where the business — not the developers — confirms that the delivered behavior matches the agreed requirements. The distinction matters:

ActivityWho runs itWhat it proves
Developer testDevelopersThe code does what the developer intended
System testQA engineersComponents work together as built
UATBusiness users and SMEsThe built solution does what the business asked for

For BrightLogistics, UAT is where a real dispatcher steps through the new lead-intake flow with real inbound leads and answers one question: does this let me move a lead from inbox to assigned in under four hours? You cannot skip UAT because the build passed its automated tests — automated tests prove the code is correct against its own inputs; UAT proves the code is correct against the business's workflows, permissions, and expectations.

UAT is a decision point, not a formality: the output is a Go/No-Go recommendation backed by exit criteria, defect records, and a signed form. Everything before built the thing right; UAT is when the business decides whether it is right.

2. UAT Explores, Scripts Confirm

UAT runs on two complementary tracks. Scripted test cases confirm that each acceptance criterion is met: they list concrete steps, the expected result, and a pass/fail outcome. Exploratory testing sends trained users into the system without a script to find surprises — the weird combination of leads, the unusual discount, the workflow no one scripted because no one planned for it.

Test caseStepsExpected result
TC-010 Route high-priority caseCreate a Case, set high priority, saveAssignee = tier-1 queue
TC-011 Story completion moves statusMark story Done with criteria filledStatus = Done
TC-012 Duplicate lead suppressedInsert lead with same email + companySecond attempt warned

Use both deliberately: scripts earn the criteria, exploration wins user confidence. Every surprise found in exploration becomes a new scripted regression case for future releases.

3. Building the UAT Plan

The UAT plan states the scope, the scenarios, the participants, the schedule, and — most importantly — the exit criteria, agreed before testing starts. Agreeing exit criteria in advance is what makes UAT a decision instead of an argument: you cannot move the finished line after the race.

A complete UAT plan for BrightLogistics contains:

SectionContent
ScopeThe modules under test: lead capture, routing, approval, duplicate handling
Out of scopeBilling migration (deferred decision D-105)
ScenariosThe ranked gap list from Phase 11 converted to test themes
ParticipantsDispatcher SMEs, Ops lead, one billing user, the BA as scribe
DataSandbox data that mirrors real lead volumes and mix
Schedule3 cycles of 2 days each, with daily defect triage
Exit criteria100% critical pass, 100% high pass or formally deferred, all must-have stories verified

The plan names one UAT coordinator who runs the triage and one business owner who signs off — the same RACI discipline from Phase 2. The BA does not sign; the business does. The BA's job is to keep the evidence honest.

4. Anatomy of a Test Case

A test case on UAT_Test_Case__c is a small, repeatable experiment. Give it a structure a stranger can reproduce:

md
TC-101  Reject quote above authority threshold
Linked: R-106 (two-level approval), Story S-088
Precondition: logged in as Sales Manager with approval authority level 1
Steps:
  1. Open Opportunity QUOTE-9021 (value $48,000, over $40,000 threshold)
  2. Submit for approval
  3. Open the first approver's Inbox and approve
  4. Open the second approver's Inbox
Expected result 1: First approval step advances; record shows "First approved"
Expected result 2: Second approval step appears and is required before approval completes
Actual result        : ____
Status__c            : Passed / Failed / Blocked
Severity__c (if fail): ____

Every case carries the story lookup to User_Story__c, so it inherits traceability back to the requirement. Fields you will use constantly: Status__c (Passed / Failed / Blocked), Severity__c (the impact if it fails), and Signed_Off__c (the flag that accumulates toward the go-live gate). Write expected results as observables — "second approver sees the request" — never as intentions like "approval works correctly".

5. From Acceptance Criteria to Test Script

The acceptance criteria written in Phase 6 are a ready-made test script. A Given/When/Then criterion maps one-to-one onto test case steps:

Acceptance criterion (Given/When/Then)Test case element
Given a lead with a company matching an existing LeadPrecondition + test data
When the dispatcher saves the new leadStep
Then the duplicate rule warns before saveExpected result

If a criterion cannot be scripted, either it is untestable or a step is missing — fix both before UAT, not during. BrightLogistics reviews every "must-have" story for scriptability in the same session that builds the plan.

6. Traceability: Requirement to Story to Test Case

Traceability is the backbone of UAT: every requirement covered by at least one story, every story by at least one test case. The chain answers three questions at any moment:

  1. Which requirements are not yet verified? (coverage report)
  2. Which requirement caused this failed test? (root cause)
  3. What regressed after this fix? (impact analysis)

The reporting pattern is a report with UAT_Test_Case__c as the primary object, grouped by the related story and requirement, showing Status__c per row. Missing rows are the traceability gaps. When BrightLogistics enters UAT with 14 requirements, the coverage report must show at least 14 test relationships — one or more per requirement — before the first test is even executed.

Self-check: A story has no UAT test case. What is the traceability state? A coverage gap — the requirement is not verifiable end to end until a test case exists.

7. Defect Management

A defect is simply "expected result not achieved." It is a fact about the test run, not a judgment about the team. When a test fails, UAT_Test_Case__c is set to Failed, and the after-save UAT_Defect_Logging flow creates a change-request Case carrying the failed test case's link and Severity__c so the defect is never orphaned. The service behind this is UATDefectLoggerService.cls:

apex
// UATTestCaseService: Failed -> defect Case, Passed -> sign-off
if (tc.Status__c == 'Failed') {
  // After-save Flow UAT_Defect_Logging creates a change-request Case
  // with the failed test case linked and Severity__c copied over.
}
if (tc.Status__c == 'Passed') {
  tc.Signed_Off__c = true;   // accumulates toward the go-live gate
}

One rule keeps defects honest: never fix a defect inside UAT without a decision. Log it, triage it, decide, implement, then re-run the exact same steps. Fixing "just this once" poisons the evidence — you no longer know what the passing run proves.

8. Severity vs Priority: Two Different Numbers

A defect carries two labels that are easy to confuse and important to separate. Severity measures the impact of the defect on the business. Priority measures the order in which it will be fixed. A severe defect is not automatically urgent, and a non-severe defect can still be urgent.

SeverityMeaningBrightLogistics example
CriticalBlocks business entirelyA dispatcher cannot save a new Lead
HighMajor function brokenLeads route to the wrong tier
MediumWorkaround existsApproval email contains the wrong subject line
LowCosmeticButton spacing on the routing screen

Priority depends on impact × exposure: a Critical defect hitting every dispatch is Priority 1; one on a rare screen may be Priority 3. Logging both numbers lets triage sort by (severity, priority), not volume.

9. Running the UAT Cycle

A UAT cycle is a short, strictly managed loop:

  1. Prepare: agree exit criteria, load test data, brief participants.
  2. Run: execute scripted cases in order; exploratory sessions in parallel.
  3. Log: every Failed case triggers the defect flow automatically.
  4. Triage: daily (or twice daily) defect review — severity, priority, fix decision, owner.
  5. Retest: after fixes, re-run the exact failing steps on the same test case.
  6. Sign off: passed cases accumulate the Signed_Off__c flag module by module.

BrightLogistics runs a two-day cycle three times, triaging between cycles, with the business owner reviewing cumulative sign-off per module each time. Test the current build only — retesting old cycles wastes time and misleads sign-off counts.

10. Sign-off and the Go/No-Go Gate

Go-live is authorized by evidence, not vibes. The go/no-go gate stands at the intersection of the exit criteria and the collected signatures:

md
Go/No-Go gate checklist
- [ ] 100% Critical defects resolved
- [ ] 100% High defects resolved or formally deferred
- [ ] Every must-have story passed its test case
- [ ] Sign-off form signed by Business Owner and PM
- [ ] Known-issues list published with the release

Two ideas make the gate trustworthy: deferral is a real option carrying the name of whoever accepted the risk, and sign-off is collected per module then summed into the final Go. A signed go-live form is the BA's strongest deliverable — it turns approval into a fact, not a memory.

11. UAT Metrics and Reporting

UAT produces numbers that everyone downstream wants. The dashboard described in Phase 10 becomes the live status board for the cycle:

MetricDefinitionTells you
Pass ratePassed cases / total executedIs the build converging?
Defect open countFailed cases minus retested passesIs the queue shrinking?
Requirement coverageRequirements with at least one passIs the scope verified?
Sign-off progressSigned-off modules / total modulesIs the gate in reach?

Report per module and per build. If pass rate rises but open defects stay flat, the team adds tests faster than it fixes them — freeze scenarios and retest. The dashboard keeps Greg informed with dates and numbers, no status meetings.

12. Pitfalls and the Handover to Change

Watch for the classic UAT pitfalls, all of them fixable with planning:

  • Testing without preconditions — every case runs on the wrong starting state and passes or fails for the wrong reason.
  • Fixing during the session — poisons the evidence; always log, decide, retest.
  • No exploratory time — users script-walk through the app and miss the surprises that will bite in production.
  • Moving exit criteria — the gate turns into an argument; agree the numbers up front.
  • Sign-off by the wrong person — the RACI business owner signs, not the PM, not the BA, not the developer.

When UAT completes, the results hand into Phase 13: the known-issues list becomes the release notes' "Fixed and Known," the sign-off date anchors the adoption baseline, and the training plan targets the modules where users now have real experience. The signed test cases are also your portfolio evidence — Exercise 8.1 (UAT Plan) and 8.2 (Test-Case Design) in the Phase 15 guide are exactly these artifacts, and Exercise 9.1 (Portfolio Checklist) wants them filed and dated.

Hands-On Exercises

1. Write a BrightLogistics UAT Plan

Write the UAT plan for the lead-intake release.

Steps:

  1. State scope, participants, data, schedule, and out-of-scope items.
  2. Define numeric exit criteria inspired by the Go/No-Go checklist.
  3. Name the coordinator and the business sign-off owner per RACI.

Expected result: a plan a third party can read and run without questions.

What it proves: that UAT planning is scope plus schedule plus agreed, measurable exit criteria (Exercise 8.1).

2. Design Four Test Cases from a Story

Turn one BrightLogistics story into four test cases.

Steps:

  1. Pick the "auto-assign leads" story and its acceptance criteria.
  2. Write one happy-path case, one boundary case (lead at threshold), one error case, and one permission case.
  3. Fill in preconditions, steps, and observable expected results on UAT_Test_Case__c.

Expected result: four cases with full fields and a story lookup each.

What it proves: that acceptance criteria translate one-to-one into scripts (Exercise 8.2).

3. Walk the Defect Logging Flow

Simulate a failed test and follow the automation.

Steps:

  1. Set a test case to Failed with Severity__c = High.
  2. Confirm the UAT_Defect_Logging flow creates the change-request Case and links the test case.
  3. Record the triage decision: severity, priority, fix owner, retest plan.

Expected result: a defect Case exists with source, link, and a named retest step.

What it proves: that the failed-result path is automatic and leaves no orphaned defects.

4. Run a Mini Sign-off Gate

Recreate the Go/No-Go decision on your module.

Steps:

  1. List critical/high defects that are open.
  2. Classify each as resolved, deferred (with owner), or blocking.
  3. Mark the checklist and produce a signed recommendation.

Expected result: an explicit, evidence-backed Go or No-Go with a filled checklist.

What it proves: that sign-off is a fact assembled from statuses and signatures, not a feeling.

5. Traceability Coverage Check

Build the coverage report for your test cases.

Steps:

  1. Group test cases by story and requirement.
  2. Highlight requirements with zero passing test cases.
  3. Write the one-paragraph coverage conclusion for the dashboard.

Expected result: a coverage matrix showing every requirement verified.

What it proves: that traceability is how you prove "every requirement is tested."

Key Terms Glossary

TermDefinition
UATBusiness-run testing proving the solution against agreed requirements and real scenarios
Scripted test caseA repeatable test with steps, expected result, and a pass/fail outcome
Exploratory testingFree-form user testing that discovers unscripted surprises
Exit criteriaNumeric acceptance thresholds agreed before testing begins
UAT planThe scope, scenarios, participants, schedule, and exit criteria document
PreconditionThe starting state a test case must run from
Expected resultThe observable outcome that marks a test pass
DefectA recorded case where the expected result was not achieved
SeverityThe business impact of a defect if unfixed
PriorityThe order in which defects will be fixed
RetestRe-running the exact failing steps after a fix is deployed
Go/No-Go gateThe agreed checklist that authorizes go-live
Signed_Off__cThe flag that accumulates per module toward go-live on UAT_Test_Case__c
TraceabilityThe requirement → story → test-case linkage proving coverage

Certification Checkpoints

  • I can write a UAT plan with scope, scenarios, participants, schedule, and numeric exit criteria.
  • I can convert a Given/When/Then acceptance criterion into a test script.
  • I know why traceability requires every requirement to link to at least one test case.
  • I can separate severity from priority and defend both labels on a defect.
  • I can log a failure through UAT_Defect_Logging without fixing mid-cycle.
  • I can run a retest of the exact failing steps after a fix.
  • I can produce a Go/No-Go recommendation backed by the gate checklist.
  • I have completed Exercise 8.1 (UAT Plan) and 8.2 (Test-Case Design) in Phase 15.

Summary

You learned that UAT is the business proving the build against its own requirements. You structured the phase with a UAT plan and agreed exit criteria, wrote scripted test cases that trace back to stories and requirements, logged failures through the UAT_Defect_Logging flow with severity and priority kept separate, and gated go-live on a Go/No-Go checklist with a signed acceptance form. Defects became data instead of drama, and the known-issues list and sign-off dates now feed release notes and the adoption baseline. The next step is carrying those results, and the people who produced them, through a change plan that keeps adoption as strong as the release.
